definition: Estimating per-word or per-utterance reliability of a transcript, used to gate human review, trigger clarification in voice bots, and filter pseudo-labels for semi-supervised training.
details: Estimating per-word or per-utterance reliability of a transcript, used to gate human review, trigger clarification in voice bots, and filter pseudo-labels for semi-supervised training. Needs explicit calibration: raw model probabilities are poor confidence estimates.

explainer.lead: ASR confidence scoring estimates how likely each recognized word, or an entire transcript, is to be correct. It helps speech systems decide when to trust a result, ask for clarification, send it to a human reviewer, or exclude it from training data.

tiers.eli5: Imagine a friend writing down what you say and circling any words they are unsure about. A speech recognizer can do something similar by giving words or whole sentences confidence scores. Those scores help it know when to ask again instead of confidently making a mistake.
tiers.practitioner: Use word-level scores to locate uncertain transcript spans and utterance-level scores to route whole results to clarification or human review. In semi-supervised training, the same scores can filter pseudo-labels before they are reused. Do not treat raw model probabilities as ready-made confidence scores: explicit calibration is needed.
tiers.paperLevel: For a recognized token w_i, confidence can be expressed as C(w_i), an estimate of P(w_i is correct | available recognition information); an utterance-level score C(U) estimates reliability for the whole transcript. Decisions apply thresholds to these calibrated scores for review, clarification, or pseudo-label acceptance. Raw model probabilities are poor confidence estimates without explicit calibration, and a confidence value does not itself guarantee correctness.

explainer.example: A voice bot transcribes “Book a table for two,” but assigns a low confidence score to “two.” Instead of booking immediately, it asks, “Did you say a table for two?”

usedIn.name: Transcription review
usedIn.detail: Low-confidence transcripts or words can be routed to human reviewers.

usedIn.name: Voice bots
usedIn.detail: Uncertain recognition can trigger a clarification question instead of an immediate action.

usedIn.name: Semi-supervised speech training
usedIn.detail: Confidence thresholds can filter unreliable pseudo-labels before training.

explainer.intuition: A transcript is more useful when the system also indicates which parts should not be trusted automatically. Confidence scoring turns recognition output into a reliability signal that downstream decisions can use.
howItWorks: Produce a transcript with an automatic speech recognition system.
Estimate reliability for individual words, the full utterance, or both.
Calibrate the scores rather than using raw model probabilities directly.
Compare the calibrated scores with thresholds for the intended application.
Route low-confidence results to review or clarification, or filter them from pseudo-labelled training data.
explainer.whyItMatters: Confidence scores let systems handle uncertain speech differently from reliable speech. This supports targeted human review, safer clarification in voice bots, and cleaner pseudo-labels for semi-supervised training.
misconceptions: A high raw model probability is not necessarily a well-calibrated confidence score.
A high confidence score does not guarantee that the transcript is correct.
Word-level and utterance-level confidence serve different decisions and are not interchangeable.

diagram.caption: Calibrated confidence scores route recognition output toward review, clarification, or pseudo-label filtering.
